title: Shield, dome and cone: three shapes of volcano
description: A volcano's shape is a fingerprint of its lava. Runny lava builds wide, gentle shields; sticky lava piles into domes; and alternating ash and lava stack the classic steep cone.

body.heading: Runny lava builds shields
paragraphs: Some lava is thin and fluid, flowing for many kilometres before it hardens — like the basalt eruptions of Hawaii. Layer upon layer of these long flows builds a shield volcano: enormously wide, with slopes so gentle you could walk up without noticing, named for its resemblance to a warrior's shield laid on the ground.
The same runny lava makes eruptions comparatively gentle: spectacular rivers of rock that usually move slowly enough for people to evacuate, though they destroy everything in their path.

body.heading: Sticky lava builds domes and cones
paragraphs: Thick, sticky lava barely flows at all. It oozes out and piles up over the vent as a steep lava dome, which can later collapse or explode. In between, stratovolcanoes alternate layers of ash and lava flows, building the tall, symmetrical cones of picture books — and the most explosive eruptions, because sticky lava traps gas like a cork in a bottle.
So the silhouette tells the story: gentle shield, runny lava; steep cone, trapped gas. Volcanologists read a volcano's shape the way you read a warning label.

takeaway: Volcano shapes record lava thickness: fluid lava spreads into wide shields, sticky lava piles into domes, and alternating ash and lava stack steep, explosive cones.
